sources.citation: Holzknecht, Susanne. 2001. Number and person in the Duwet language of Papua New Guinea: the obsessive case of number. In Pawley, Ross & Tryon (eds), The boy from Bundaberg, 175-192. Pacific Linguistics 514.
sources.note: About Duwet; Nafi mentioned only as a close relative sharing word-final [s]~[h]; nothing on Nafi stress.

sources.citation: Holzknecht, Susanne. 1989. The Markham languages of Papua New Guinea. Pacific Linguistics C-115. Canberra: ANU. Nafi phonology = sec. 4.2.12, p.57 (Table 4.13 + 5 notes).
sources.harvard_location: Widener Library (offsite storage), call number PL5026 .H64 1989
sources.note: Nothing. Sec. 4.2.12 (p.57) gives only the phoneme inventory (p b mb m f w d nd n s r j nj y k g ? ngg ng; vowels i e a o u) and five allophony notes (/f/ final [h]; [s]~[h] finally; [r]~[l]; /k/ backed; final /b/ -> [v]~[w]; final prenasalised stops realised as nasals). The word 'stress' occurs in the whole book only in a Duwet vowel-reduction note ('In unstressed position..') and a historical note on South/North Watut final -?; no general Markham stress rule is stated. The intro (p.50) says 'Full phonological statements are to be published at a later date'.

sources.citation: Holzknecht, Susanne C. 1988. The Markham languages of Papua New Guinea: a history of the Austronesian languages of the Markham and Ramu Valleys. PhD thesis, Australian National University.
sources.note: Same Nafi phoneme sketch as the 1989 book (Table 4.13); a full-text search for stress/accent full text for stress/accent finds no Nafi statement.

sources.citation: Hooley, Bruce A. 1971. Austronesian languages of the Morobe District, Papua New Guinea. Oceanic Linguistics 10(2): 79-151.
sources.note: Only other primary publication with first-hand data on the language (as 'Sirak'); a survey/classification with wordlists that may carry brief phonological notes. Low odds of a stress statement but it is the last unopened item.

sources.note: No written stress description exists; these elicitation/text recordings are the only material from which Nafi stress could be determined (instrumentally or by ear). Any unpublished Holzknecht field notes/phonology write-up ('full phonological statements.. to be published at a later date', PL C-115 p.50) would be the ideal find.
